topicTags: Parliament: Parliamentary sovereignty and parliamentary privilege
stem: During a debate in the House of Commons, an MP accuses a famous businessman of a serious criminal offence. The MP is interviewed outside Parliament, where he repeats the allegation. A newspaper reports the debate and the interview with the MP. The businessman wants to sue for defamation.
ask: Which of the following best summarises the legal position?

options.en: Only the MP can be sued.
Only the newspaper can be sued.
Neither the newspaper nor the MP can be sued.
The MP cannot be sued.
Both the MP and newspaper can be sued.

explanation.topic: Parliament: Parliamentary sovereignty and parliamentary privilege
explanation.en: The correct answer was E. What is said in a parliamentary proceeding, such as a debate, is protected by absolute privilege. If, however, it is repeated outside Parliament, there is no protection from defamation proceedings. Fair and accurate reports of parliamentary proceedings are protected by qualified privilege, but not the repetition of statements made outside of a parliamentary proceeding.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 2

stem: A client is an MP, who is employed as a parliamentary consultant, by the Road Transport Group, at an annual salary of £10,000. The Road Transport Group opposes proposed new restrictions on the hours worked by lorry drivers. The Group instructs their consultant MP to vote against these measures in Parliament and say that they will no longer employ him if he refuses.
ask: Which of the following best summarises the position of the client?

options.en: An MP cannot have a job with an outside body.
An MP cannot receive any payments from an outside body.
An MP can be dismissed from their consultancy with an outside body.
An MP cannot be instructed on how to vote by an outside body.
An MP can have a job with an outside body.

explanation.topic: Parliament: Parliamentary sovereignty and parliamentary privilege
explanation.en: The correct answer was D. MPs are permitted outside interests, although they must register them, but the body or person that employs them must not try to control the MP’s conduct in Parliament. If the employer told their MP how to vote, this would be a breach of parliamentary privilege and they could be punished for contempt of Parliament.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 2

stem: The prime minister wishes to appoint a key adviser as a Cabinet minister. The appointment of ministers is governed by convention.
ask: Which of the following conventions would govern this appointment?

options.en: The adviser must be a member of the House of Commons or the House of Lords.
The adviser must be a member of the House of Commons.
The adviser must be nominated by the Cabinet.
The adviser must be nominated by the prime minister’s political party.
The adviser must be a member of the House of Lords.

explanation.en: The correct answer was A. This is because convention requires a minister to be a member of either of the two Houses of Parliament. Otherwise, the minster cannot be accountable to Parliament.

stem: A civil servant in the Home Office authorises the unlawful deportation of an alleged illegal immigrant.
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate person against whom legal action should be taken?

options.en: The civil servant.
Her Majesty’s government.
The secretary of state for home affairs.
The attorney general.
The prime minister.

explanation.en: The correct answer was C. This is because the government minister in charge of the department takes legal responsibility for what happens in their department.

stem: A government minister has been convicted for driving while disqualified. The prime minister seeks advice upon whether he must require the minister to resign. The Independent Adviser on Ministerial Standards consults the Ministerial Code to advise the prime minister.
ask: Which of the following best describes the position under the code?

options.en: The minister must resign if he commits a criminal offence.
The minister must resign if he is in breach of collective responsibility.
The minister must resign if he is in breach of Cabinet confidentiality.
The minister must resign if he compromises the political impartiality of the Civil Service.
The minister must resign if he knowingly misleads Parliament.

explanation.en: The correct answer was E. This is because the Ministerial Code tells ministers what they can and cannot do, but only in this example does it require resignation. Usually, resignation is left to the discretion of the prime minister.

stem: The first minister of Northern Ireland wishes to appoint a member of his political party, John, as a minister.
ask: Which of the following best describes the procedure for doing this?

options.en: The first minister nominates John and the monarch appoints him.
The first minister appoints John.
The first minister appoints John with the agreement of the deputy first minister.
A political party in the Northern Ireland Assembly nominates John.
The first minister appoints John with the agreement of the secretary of state for Northern Ireland.

explanation.en: The correct answer was D. This is what the devolution legislation for Northern Ireland requires. It is unusual because in the government of the UK, Scotland and Wales the prime minister or first minister nominates a minister and the King appoints them.

stem: An Act of the Scottish Parliament is passed, with a simple majority, declaring that Scotland is an independent country and no longer part of the UK.
ask: Which of the following best describes the effect of this Act?

options.en: The Act would only be law in Scotland.
The Act would not be law because it is outside the legislative competence of the Scottish Parliament.
The Act would not be law because a two-thirds majority of the Scottish Parliament is required.
The Act would be law if the Supreme Court agreed.
The Act would be law for all of the UK.

explanation.en: The correct answer was B. This is because the devolution legislation for Scotland does not allow the Scottish Parliament to legislate on the Union with England or the constitution. Remember that the devolved legislatures have limited powers.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 3

topicTags: The Crown and the royal prerogative
stem: After a general election, no political party has a majority in the House of Commons. The existing prime minister wants to carry on in office.
ask: Which of the following statements best summarises what the monarch should do?

options.en: The monarch should dismiss the prime minister.
The monarch should appoint the leader of the largest political party in the House of Commons as prime minister.
The monarch should agree that the prime minister can carry on in office.
The monarch should advise the prime minister to form a coalition government of the two largest parties in the House of Commons.
The monarch should allow the political parties in the House of Commons to negotiate.

explanation.topic: The Crown and the royal prerogative
explanation.en: The correct answer was E. This is because the convention is that the prime minister should be able to command a majority in the House of Commons. If there is no obvious candidate, the parties in the Commons would be left to negotiate a coalition or minority government. The monarch should not become involved.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 4

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 4
topicTags: The Crown and the royal prerogative
stem: A close relative of the monarch is prosecuted for dangerous driving.
ask: Which of the following best summarises the legal position?

options.en: The relative can be prosecuted, but not sentenced to imprisonment.
The relative has immunity from the criminal law.
The Crown Proceedings Act 1947 means that the law cannot be enforced against the relative.
By convention, members of the royal family are not prosecuted for minor offences.
The relative has no legal immunities or privileges.

explanation.topic: The Crown and the royal prerogative
explanation.en: The correct answer was E. This is because only the monarch is above the law. The rest of the royal family have no legal immunities. Be careful. You were asked about the legal position, not about convention.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 4

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 4
topicTags: The Crown and the royal prerogative
stem: An overseas possession of the Crown has been invaded by a foreign state. The government decides to send armed forces to recapture the territory. The government requisitions a ship, belonging to a private company, to transport soldiers to the possession and refuses to pay any compensation.
ask: Which of the following best summarises the legal position?

options.en: The government has no legal power to requisition a ship.
The government has the legal power to requisition a ship.
The government has the legal power to requisition a ship, but must pay compensation.
The government has no legal power to requisition a ship, without the authority of an Act of Parliament.
The government has no legal power to requisition a ship, without the permission of Parliament.

explanation.topic: The Crown and the royal prerogative
explanation.en: The correct answer was C. This because the government has a prerogative power to requisition property for use in military action. Case law states that compensation must be paid.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 4

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 4
topicTags: The Crown and the royal prerogative
stem: A man has been refused a passport on the grounds that he is not a UK citizen. He believes that he can prove that he is a UK citizen.
ask: Which of the following best summarises the man’s legal position?

options.en: If the man can prove he is a UK citizen, the government must give him a passport.
The man cannot challenge a decision made under the royal prerogative.
If the man can prove he is a UK citizen, the government has a discretion to give him a passport.
If the man can prove he is a UK citizen, the government must have a valid reason for refusing him a passport.
The man cannot challenge the citizenship or the passport decision.

explanation.topic: The Crown and the royal prerogative
explanation.en: The correct answer was D. This is because although the granting of a passport is a prerogative power, refusal could be judicially reviewed if there was no legal or rational reason for rejection.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 4

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 4
topicTags: The Crown and the royal prerogative
stem: A volcanic eruption causes an emergency on a Caribbean island. The prime minister wants to send armed forces to the island to provide humanitarian assistance to the islanders.
ask: Which of the following is the best description of the legal position?

options.en: The prime minister needs the agreement of the House of Commons.
The prime minister needs legislation to authorise this.
The prime minister can send the armed forces, but must justify it to the House of Commons.
The prime minister needs the agreement of the monarch.
The prime minister has the power to do this and does not need any authorisation.

explanation.topic: The Crown and the royal prerogative
explanation.en: The correct answer was C. This is because a convention has developed in the twenty-first century that the Commons must authorise the deployment of the armed forces abroad for military action. This does not apply to emergencies or humanitarian actions, where the government is merely accountable to Parliament.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 4

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 5
stem: A client is being tried for an offence under an Act of Parliament that was not in force on the date when the offence was committed.
ask: Which of the following decisions would the court make?

options.en: The court would declare the Act of Parliament void.
The court would order Parliament to either bring the Act into force or repeal it.
The court would acquit the client.
The court would make a declaration of incompatibility under the Human Rights Act 1998.
The court would convict the client.

explanation.en: The correct answer was C. This is because if an Act of Parliament is not in force it is not the law. It is a basic principle of statutory interpretation that an Act of Parliament is not retrospective unless it explicitly says so.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 5

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 5
stem: The largest political party in the House of Lords is opposed to a Bill that has passed all its stages in the House of Commons and wants to prevent this Bill from becoming law.
ask: Which of the following statements best summarises the legal position?

options.en: The House of Lords can vote against the Bill and prevent it becoming law.
The House of Lords can only amend the Bill, but not prevent it from becoming law.
The House of Lords may refer the Bill to a Joint Committee of the Commons and Lords.
The House of Lords may delay the Bill, but not prevent it from becoming law.
The House of Lords can vote against the Bill and then royal assent will be refused.

explanation.en: The correct answer was D. This is because the House of Lords cannot prevent the House of Commons passing an Act, but only delay the Commons for a year. Usually, the two Houses compromise and agree amendments, because the government does not want to wait a year for its legislation.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 5

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 5
stem: A haulage firm objects to some new regulations made by the secretary of state for transport. They have been approved by both Houses of Parliament, but the haulage firm can prove that the enabling Act does not give the secretary of state the power to make these regulations. The firm seeks a judicial review.
ask: Which of the following best summarises the legal position?

options.en: The secretary of state has an inherent power to make regulations.
The secretary of state may use the royal prerogative to make regulations.
The secretary of state’s regulations have been approved by Parliament and are legal.
The secretary of state’s regulations are illegal and void.
The secretary of state’s regulations cannot be judicially reviewed.

explanation.en: The correct answer was D. This is because there must be a power under an enabling or parent Act, which allows the secretary of state to make the regulations. Without such a power, Parliament’s approval is irrelevant.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 5

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 5
stem: In a court case, the Supreme Court has declared that a particular section of an Act of Parliament is incompatible with the human rights protected under the Human Rights Act 1998. The secretary of state for home affairs wishes to remove the incompatibility as soon as possible.
ask: Which of the following courses of action would take the least time?

options.en: The secretary of state could ask Parliament to repeal the offending Act of Parliament.
The secretary of state could ask Parliament to amend the offending Act of Parliament.
The secretary of state could ask the Supreme Court to reconsider the case.
The secretary of state could ask Parliament to repeal the Human Rights Act 1998.
The secretary of state could ask Parliament to make a Remedial Order.

explanation.en: The correct answer was E. This is because there is a ‘fast-track’ procedure under s 10 of the Human Rights Act 1998, where a Remedial Order may be made that can repeal or amend an Act of Parliament. As it is delegated legislation, it does not have to go through the numerous stages required for a parliamentary Bill.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 5

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 5
stem: A new set of regulations has been made by the secretary of state using a statutory power that requires the affirmative resolution procedure. The House of Commons and the House of Lords have not voted to approve these regulations. A client wishes to judicially review these regulations.
ask: Which of the following best summarises the legal position?

options.en: The court would declare the regulations void for procedural impropriety.
The court would declare the regulations valid, as minor defects in procedure are immaterial.
The court would refer the regulations back to Parliament for approval.
The court would refuse to judicially review legislation.
The court would ask the secretary of state to confirm that he approves the regulations.

explanation.en: The correct answer was A. This is because procedural impropriety is one of the bases of judicial review. Failure to comply with the laying requirements laid down in the parent Act might lead to the court declaring the regulations void.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 5

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 6
stem: The police learn that a man plans to lead a public procession through the streets of a major town to protest police violence. He has not notified the police of the procession.
ask: Which of the following best summarises the legal position?

options.en: The failure to notify means that the police may ban the public procession.
The failure to notify means that the police may ban the public procession with the permission of the home secretary.
The failure to notify means that the police may ban the public procession with the permission of the local council and home secretary.
The failure to notify means that the police may impose conditions on the route of the procession.
The failure to notify means that the police may prosecute the man for an offence.

explanation.en: The correct answer was E. This is because the power to impose conditions depends upon the senior officer of police reasonably believing that the procession may result in serious public disorder, serious damage to property or serious disruption to the life of the community or that the purpose of the organisers is to intimidate others. To ban the procession, the chief officer of police must reasonably believe that there will be serious public disorder. Failure to notify is just an offence that may be committed by the organiser.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 6

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 6
stem: A man is a supporter of United and attends a football match against City. When he leaves the ground, he and his fellow United supporters are stopped from walking to the railway station by the police. In the previous fixture between United and City there had been many violent clashes between the supporters of the two clubs. The police tell the United supporters that they must wait one hour for the City supporters to disperse. The man refuses to obey the police officer, tries to push past him and is arrested.
ask: Which of the following best summarises the legal position?

options.en: The police have no power to deprive the man of his liberty.
The police may arrest for breach of the peace.
The police may arrest for obstruction of the highway.
The police may arrest because this is an unauthorised public procession.
The police may arrest because this is an unauthorised public assembly.

explanation.en: The correct answer was B. This is because the previous violence makes it reasonable to believe that violence might recur. The police may take reasonable steps to prevent this happening. This includes temporarily detaining people and if they refuse, arresting them.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 6

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 6
stem: Two men are drunk when they leave a public house and begin fighting. A barmaid leaving work sees them, is frightened and calls the police. A police officer arrests both men.
ask: Which of the following offences have the two men committed?

options.en: Riot.
Violent disorder.
Affray.
Fear or provocation of violence.
Harassment, alarm or distress.

explanation.en: The correct answer was C. This is because 12 persons are required for riot, 3 for violent disorder and we are not told that either party has used threatening, abusive or insulting words. Two persons fighting could be an affray and the barmaid is a person of reasonable firmness, who might fear for her safety.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 6

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 6
stem: A crowd gathers outside the constituency office of an MP to protest against government policy. They shout loud slogans and play loud music frightening the staff in the office and making it difficult for them to work.
ask: Which of the following best summarises the legal position?

options.en: A senior officer of police can disperse the crowd because it is a breach of the peace.
The chief officer of police can apply to the local council to ban the protest as it is a trespassory assembly.
A senior officer of police can limit the duration of this public assembly.
A police officer can arrest the protesters for threatening behaviour.
A police officer can arrest the protesters for riot.

explanation.en: The correct answer was C. It is not a trespassory assembly because the protesters have not entered the constituency office. Breach of the peace, threatening behaviour and riot all require violence or a theat of violence. A senior officer of police has powers to control a public assembly if they reasonably believe that there may be a serious disruption to the life of the community. This includes noise which is likely to intimidate, harass or cause alarm or distress.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 6

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 6
stem: A large crowd of people, who support animal rights, gather on the pavement outside a shop selling animals. They display signs and shout slogans indicating their disapproval of this trade, but do not use or threaten any violence or make any insulting remarks. Many passers-by stop to watch, and the street is completely blocked to people and vehicles. The police ask the protesters to disperse and when they refuse, arrest them.
ask: Which of the following crimes have the protesters committed?

options.en: Obstruction of the highway.
Aggravated trespass.
Causing harassment, alarm or distress.
Fear or provocation of violence.
Breach of the peace.

explanation.en: The correct answer was A. A small demonstration on the highway may be permitted, but blocking the highway is not allowed. They are not trespassing nor using violence or threatening words, so the other offences do not apply.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 6

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 7
stem: A local council refuses a building firm planning permission to build an estate. The firm appeals, but the planning inspector upholds the refusal. The planning inspector is the brother of the chair of the council. The building firm seeks judicial review of the decision to refuse planning permission.
ask: Which of the following arguments would be the most likely to succeed?

options.en: The refusal is irrational.
The refusal is illegal.
The refusal is a breach of legitimate expectation.
The refusal is a fettering of discretion.
The refusal is a breach of natural justice.

explanation.en: The correct answer was E. The chair of the council is related to the planning inspector. This would give the appearance of bias to the fair- minded and informed observer. There is no need to prove that there was actual bias, just a real possibility of it.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 7

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 7
stem: The secretary of state has power under the [fictitious] Carbon Act 2021 to make regulations on the type of fuel used by airliners, as he sees fit. The Act requires that, before making the regulations, the secretary of state shall consult any employer appearing to him to be a substantial employer of persons engaged in aircraft manufacturing. The secretary of state makes regulations, but does not consult a company that is the largest aircraft manufacturer in the UK.
ask: Which of the following best summarises the legal position?

options.en: The secretary of state has the power to make any regulations that he wants.
The secretary of state has absolute discretion on whom he consults.
The secretary of state has a duty to consult the company.
The secretary of state may make any regulations he wants, as long as they are neither illegal nor irrational.
The secretary of state may not make the regulations without the agreement of the company.

explanation.en: The correct answer was C. This is because although the secretary of state has discretion upon whom he consults, he must exercise it in a reasonable way. He cannot ignore the largest employer.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 7

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 7
stem: A local council decides that all children in its schools should receive free school meals, irrespective of their family income. The council raises the rate of council tax to pay for this.
ask: Which of the following would have sufficient interest to apply for judicial review of the decision?

options.en: Any legal person.
Any incorporated or statutory body.
The secretary of state for education.
Local council taxpayers.
The prime minister.

explanation.en: The correct answer was D. This is because the local taxpayers are directly affected by the decision, because they must pay more council tax. None of the other candidates are affected by the decision.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 7

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 7
stem: Local councils have the power to grant licences to drive a taxi. A woman applies for a licence but is told by the council that it is not their policy to grant any more taxi licences for their area.
ask: Which of the following would be the woman’s best course of action?

options.en: The woman should apply for judicial review.
The woman should sue for breach of contract.
The woman should apply to the European Court of Human Rights.
The woman should be advised that the council has the power to refuse licence applications.
The woman should sue the council for negligent performance of their duties.

explanation.en: The correct answer was A. This is because the refusal to grant any licences is a fettering of discretion, which makes the decision illegal. Judicial review is the correct procedure to raise this issue.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 7

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 7
stem: The NHS provides a home for seven severely ill patients and has assured them that this accommodation will be available for the rest of their lives. Because of a policy change, the NHS decides to close this home and transfer the seven patients to local council care. The patients object to this change and apply for judicial review.
ask: Which of the following best summarises the legal position?

options.en: The patients do not have sufficient interest.
The NHS may move the patients if it is in the public interest.
The NHS has no obligation to consult the patients.
The NHS has no legal power to make this decision.
The NHS is not a public body.

explanation.en: The correct answer was B. This is because, although the NHS have made a promise to a small group of people, they will not have raised a substantive legitimate expectation, if the NHS can show that they had sound policy reasons for making the decision and this is not unfair to the claimants.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 7

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 8
stem: The Supreme Court has made a declaration that a section of an Act of Parliament is incompatible with human rights.
ask: Which of the following statements best summarises the legal position?

options.en: Parliament is obliged to repeal the offending section.
Parliament may repeal the offending section.
Parliament may refer the matter back to the Supreme Court.
Parliament may wait for the result of any appeal to the European Court of Human Rights.
Parliament is obliged to compensate the complainant who brought the case.

explanation.en: The correct answer was B. This is because Parliament is sovereign. The courts cannot tell Parliament what it must do.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 8

textbookReferences.book: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law

publisherReference.text: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law, Chapter 8

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 8
stem: A client alleges that his human rights have been violated and wishes to apply to the European Court of Human Rights.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes how the application should be made?

options.en: The client’s case must be referred to the European Court of Human Rights by the Supreme Court.
The client’s case may be referred to the European Court of Human Rights by any UK court or tribunal.
The client must appeal from the final decision of a UK court.
The client may apply to the European Court of Human Rights.
The client’s case may be referred to the European Court of Human Rights by the High Court or any higher court.

explanation.en: The correct answer was D. This is because the UK is a party to the ECHR and must accept the right of victims to complain to that court. However, there is no route of appeal linking the UK courts to the European Court of Human Rights.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 8

textbookReferences.book: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 8
stem: Section 2 of the Human Rights Act 1998 states that ‘a court or tribunal determining a question which has arisen under this Act in connection with a Convention right must take into account any judgment of the European Court of Human Rights’.
ask: Which of the following statements is the most accurate interpretation of the meaning of these words?

options.en: A court or tribunal must follow a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights.
A court or tribunal may choose to follow a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights.
A court or tribunal should normally follow a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights.
A court or tribunal must consider a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights.
A court or tribunal must not follow a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights.

explanation.en: The correct answer was C. The UK courts have interpreted s 2 to mean that the UK courts should normally follow decisions of the European Court of Human Rights.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 8

textbookReferences.book: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 8
stem: Under the Human Rights Act 1998 it is unlawful for a public authority to act in a way that is incompatible with a convention right. A ‘victim of the unlawful act’ may bring proceedings against the authority.
ask: Which of the following best describes the meaning of victim?

options.en: A claimant who is aggrieved by the unlawful act.
A claimant who wishes to stop the unlawful act.
A claimant who has suffered physical harm from the unlawful act.
A claimant who has suffered financial loss from the unlawful act.
A claimant who has been personally affected by the unlawful act.

explanation.en: The correct answer was E. This is the definition adopted by the European Court of Human Rights. Section 7(6) of the Human Rights Act 1998 states that UK courts should use the same test.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 8

textbookReferences.book: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law

publisherReference.text: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law, Chapter 8

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 8
stem: Under the Human Rights Act 1998 claims may be brought against a ‘public authority’.
ask: Which of the following statements best defines the meaning of public authority?

options.en: A public authority is a person (natural or legal) who receives public funding.
A public authority is a person (natural or legal) who performs a governmental function.
A public authority is a person (natural or legal) who has statutory powers.
A public authority is a person (natural or legal) who performs functions of a public nature.
A public authority is a person (natural or legal) who performs a public service.

explanation.en: The correct answer was D. That is the definition in the Act. The other answers are the factors that a court should consider when deciding whether a person is a public authority.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 8

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 9
stem: A client is involved in a legal dispute and wishes to know whether an article of the Trade and Cooperation Agreement between the UK and EU can be enforced in a national court.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes how an article is enforced?

options.en: Depending upon the wording, the article may be directly applicable.
Depending upon the wording, the article has direct effect.
Depending upon the wording, the article has horizontal direct effect.
Depending upon the wording, the article has vertical direct effect.
Depending upon the wording, the article has vertical and horizontal direct effect.

explanation.en: The correct answer was E. Although the UK has left the EU, it has agreed that articles of the Trade and Cooperation Agreement can have direct effect, meaning that they are enforceable in a UK court. Articles have both vertical and horizontal direct effect.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 9

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 9
stem: A man was unaware that EU law still had any effect in the UK, so you need to explain what ‘assimilated law’ is.
ask: Which of the following statements most accurately describes assimilated law?

options.en: assimilated law is the EU law that applied when the UK joined the EU.
assimilated law is the EU law that was implemented by delegated legislation.
assimilated law is the EU law that applied before leaving the EU.
assimilated law is the EU law passed by the European Parliament.
assimilated law is the EU law made applicable by the Withdrawal Agreement.

explanation.en: The correct answer was C. The UK kept the EU law that applied in the UK on 31 December 2020. Retained EU law, that has not been specifically repealed, has now been converted into assimilated law.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 9

textbookReferences.book: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law

publisherReference.text: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law, Chapter 9

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 9
stem: What was once EU law is now known as assimilated law in the UK.
ask: Which of the following statements is the most accurate description of how the UK courts may interpret assimilated law?

options.en: A UK court may refer questions of assimilated law to the CJEU.
A UK court is bound by decisions of the CJEU on assimilated law.
A UK court is bound to follow previous decisions of a UK court on assimilated law.
A UK court may depart from previous decisions of UK courts and the CJEU on assimilated law.
A higher UK court may depart from previous decisions of UK courts and the CJEU on assimilated law.

explanation.en: The correct answer was E. This is because UK courts may no longer refer questions of what was once EU law to the CJEU and are no longer bound by EU law. However, the lower courts are still bound by past precedents defining the meaning of EU law. As is usual in the precedent system, only the higher courts, the Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court, may change past precedents.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 9

textbookReferences.book: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law

publisherReference.text: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law, Chapter 9

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 9
stem: EU law remains in force in the UK as ‘assimilated law’. If assimilated law conflicts with UK law, which source of law must UK courts follow?
ask: Which of the following statements is the most accurate statement of the legal position?

options.en: UK law has supremacy over assimilated law.
Assimilated law has supremacy over UK law.
Assimilated law has supremacy over UK law enacted before leaving the EU.
UK law has supremacy over assimilated law unless the assimilated law protects human rights.
Assimilated law has supremacy over UK case law but not UK statute law.

explanation.en: The correct answer was A. When the UK left the EU, retained EU law had supremacy over UK Acts of Parliament enacted before leaving the UK. When retained EU law was converted into assimilated law, assimilated law had no supremacy over UK law. The normal position of a UK Act of Parliament being supreme over any other source of law was restored. EU general principles of law protecting human rights no longer apply in the UK and even the Human Rights Act 1998 could be repealed.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Constitutional and Administrative Law · Chapter 9

stem: The UK completed its Withdrawal Agreement (the Trade and Cooperation Agreement) with the EU in 2020. The UK accepted that the Withdrawal Agreement could be enforced in UK courts.
ask: Which of the following does the Withdrawal Agreement allow claimants in the UK courts to do?

options.en: Enforce rights created under the Withdrawal Agreement.
Enforce rights created under EU regulations.
Enforce rights created under EU directives.
Enforce decisions made by the CJEU.
Enforce rights created under EU decisions.

explanation.en: The correct answer was A. This is because the UK agreed in the Withdrawal Agreement to allow provisions of the Agreement that meet the conditions for direct effect under EU law to be enforced in UK courts.

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 1
topicTags: Starting a new business: types of business medium
stem: A client wishes to set up business on their own, providing light gardening services. The client is keen to keep things as straightforward as possible and to minimise costs. They do not foresee a substantial capital outlay and they have no plans to take on employees or to borrow money.
ask: Which of the following best describes the type of business medium the client should choose for their business and why?

options.en: A private limited company. This is because there is little administrative burden in setting up and running a private limited company.

A sole trader. Although limited liability would be of benefit to the client, their needs are straightforward and their investment and overheads would not

be substantial. The additional burdens of starting and running a limited company would not be justified.
A limited company in any event. The benefits of separate personality and limited liability are so great that they outweigh all other considerations.

A private limited company. The client will be able to separate ownership and control and grant floating charges over the company’s assets when they

wish to expand the business.
A public limited company. It will give the client better flexibility to expand and will enable shares to be offered to the public.

explanation.topic: Starting a new business: types of business medium
explanation.en: The correct answer was B. Although separate personality and limited liability have clear benefits, they are not the client’s main concern, particularly in view of the low capital outlay/risk. Therefore, option C is incorrect. The additional costs of forming and managing a company would be unjustified, making option A incorrect. Option D is incorrect as separation of ownership and control would be unnecessarily complicated, and they have no plans to borrow money, so the ability to grant floating charges is not a concern. Option E is incorrect as a public limited company (plc) would be even less appropriate than a private company; they have no desire to offer shares to the public and would be unlikely to meet the minimum capital requirements.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 1

topicTags: Starting a new business: types of business medium
stem: A client wishes to start up a manufacturing business with a long-standing friend and business associate. The pair plan to buy premises, employ several staff, expand very quickly and trade internationally. In the medium term, the pair will need to borrow considerable funds.
ask: Which of the following best describes the type of business medium the client and their friend should choose?

options.en: A private limited company.
A partnership.
A public limited company.
A limited liability partnership.
A private company, limited by guarantee.

explanation.topic: Starting a new business: types of business medium
explanation.en: The correct answer was A. The ambitious plans, nature of the business and need to borrow make a private limited company the obvious choice. There are likely to be significant liabilities and the ability to grant floating charges will be a clear advantage. Option B would be inappropriate as partners have unlimited liability and partnerships cannot grant floating charges. Limited companies are more recognised across the world than LLPs, which makes option D incorrect. A plc would be inappropriate in the short term as there are no plans to offer shares to the public (which makes option C incorrect). Option E is incorrect as a private company limited by guarantee would be more appropriate for a non-profit-making entity.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 1

stem: A client holds 10,000 £1 ordinary shares in a private limited company, representing a 5% shareholding. The shares are fully paid and the company is being wound up, with substantial debts.
ask: How much will the client be required to contribute on winding-up?

options.en: The client will not be required to contribute on winding-up.
The client will be required to contribute 5% of the company’s outstanding debt.
The client will be required to contribute £10,000.
The client’s liability will be unlimited.
The client will be required to contribute towards the costs of winding-up.

explanation.topic: Starting a new business: types of business medium
explanation.en: The correct answer was A. The client’s liability will be limited to any amount unpaid on their shares, which in this case is nothing. Therefore, options B, C, D and E are incorrect. The client would only be required to contribute on winding-up if the shares were not fully paid. In these circumstances, liability would be limited to the unpaid amount.

topicTags: Starting a new business: types of business medium
stem: A client is a sole trader whose business is in financial difficulty. However, they have substantial personal assets and are keen to ascertain their liability for the debts of the business.
ask: Which of the following best describes the client’s liability?

options.en: The business is a separate legal person, and the client will be able to keep their personal assets separate.
The client will be personally liable for the debts of the business.
The client’s liability will be limited to the amount they contributed to the business.
The client will be jointly and severally liable for the debts of the business.
The client will not be liable as the business has not been registered at Companies House.

explanation.topic: Starting a new business: types of business medium
explanation.en: The correct answer was B. The client’s liability will be personal, without limit, as the business is unincorporated and does not have separate legal personality. Therefore, options A and C are incorrect. There is no requirement to register the business at Companies House, so option E is incorrect. Joint and several liability is inappropriate for a sole trader but would be relevant if the client were a partner. Therefore, option D is incorrect.

topicTags: Starting a new business: types of business medium
stem: A client is looking to set up a manufacturing business with two friends who are both experienced executives. They plan to expand quickly, have substantial borrowings and appoint over 50 employees. The client is happy not to be involved in the day-to-day management of the business, but he wants to make sure that his liability is limited to his investment. The client may also wish to sell his share in the business on his retirement in a few years’ time.
ask: Which of the following best describes the type of business medium the client and his two friends should choose?

options.en: A private company, limited by shares.
A partnership.
A public limited company.
A limited liability partnership.
A private company, limited by guarantee.

explanation.topic: Starting a new business: types of business medium
explanation.en: The correct answer was A. The client’s key concerns are having limited liability, not being involved in the day-to-day management of the business and having transferrable shares. Therefore, option B is incorrect. The board structure (separation of ownership and control) and ambitious plans make this the obvious choice. There will be significant benefit to limited liability and the ability to grant floating charges. A public company would be less appropriate, although it would be possible to re-register as a public company later. Therefore, option C is incorrect. Companies limited by guarantee are usually non-profit-making entities, so option E is incorrect. Option D is incorrect as limited companies are more widely recognised than LLPs for trading purposes.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 1

stem: Two clients start a business together. They each invest 50% of the capital and share profits equally. After a number of years, the business makes a loss.
ask: Have the two clients been in partnership together?

options.en: Yes, because they are in business together with a view to making a profit.
Yes, but only because they agreed to invest equal amounts of capital.
No, because they have not entered into a formal written partnership agreement.
No, because the partnership has not been registered at Companies House.
No, because they did not agree on how losses should be shared between them.

explanation.en: The correct answer was A, as the s 1 PA criteria are met. Equal investment in capital, agreement as to how profits and losses are to be shared, and registration at Companies House are not requirements. Therefore, options B, E and D are incorrect. A formal partnership agreement is not required, but one is usually recommended. Therefore, option C is also incorrect.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 2

stem: A client seeks advice from a solicitor in setting up a partnership business.
ask: Which of the following most accurately describes the position under the Partnership Act 1890, in the absence of an express or implied agreement to the contrary?

options.en:
Partners will have an equal share of income profits, retirement of a partner will not dissolve the partnership, all partners are entitled to take part in the

management of the business and a rogue partner may not be expelled by majority vote.

Partners will have an equal share of income profits, retirement of a partner will dissolve the partnership and a rogue partner may be expelled by

majority vote.

Partners will have an equal share of income profits, retirement of a partner will dissolve the partnership, all partners are entitled to take part in the

management of the business and a rogue partner may not be expelled by majority vote.

Partners will receive income profits proportionate to their capital share, retirement of a partner will not dissolve the partnership and all partners are

entitled to take part in the management of the business.

Partners will receive income profits proportionate to their capital share, retirement of a partner will not dissolve the partnership and a rogue partner

may not be expelled by majority vote.

explanation.en: The correct answer was C. Partners will have an equal share of income profits regardless of capital input. Therefore, options D and E are incorrect on this point. Retirement of a partner will dissolve the partnership, therefore, options A, D and E are incorrect here. All partners are entitled to take part in the management of the business and a rogue partner may not be expelled by majority vote. Therefore, option B is also incorrect in this final respect.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 2

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 2
stem: A client starts a partnership business with a friend, and they make unequal capital contributions. One of the partners works full-time for the business and the other works part-time. There is no formal written partnership agreement or any agreement as to how income and capital profits will be shared.
ask: Which of the following best describes the position on the share of income and capital profits?

options.en: Income and capital profits will be shared in accordance with the partners’ respective capital contributions.
Income and capital profits will be shared in accordance with the hours worked by each partner in the business.
Income profits will be shared according to the hours worked by each partner and capital profits will be shared equally.
The partners must enter into a formal written partnership agreement as the Partnership Act 1890 does not make any provision for this type of situation.
Income profits will be shared equally, although it will most probably be implied that capital will be shared in proportion to the contributions made.

explanation.en: The correct answer was E. Income profits will be shared equally, irrespective of partners’ capital contributions and their hours worked. Therefore, options A, B and C are incorrect. It will most probably be implied that capital is shared in proportion to the contributions made, also making options A, B and C incorrect. Although a partnership agreement would be advisable in these circumstances, it is not a requirement, so option D is incorrect.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 2

stem: A client is a partner in a bakery business and enters into a transaction to buy a conservatory for his home, with partnership money.
ask: Which of the following best describes the liability of the firm for this transaction?

options.en:
The partnership as a whole will be liable. Individual partners, as joint owners of the business, always have authority to bind the firm, as agents of it.

They do not need to act jointly.

Only the contracting partner will be liable. Individual partners, despite being joint owners of the business, do not have authority to bind the firm, as

agents of it. They must make decisions jointly.

If the transaction was entered into with actual or apparent authority on the part of the contracting partner, the firm will be liable. It is unlikely that there

will be apparent authority as the deal did not relate to the type of business in which the partnership normally deals.

If the transaction was entered into with actual or apparent authority on the part of the contracting partner, the firm will be liable. It is unlikely that there

will be apparent authority unless the third party actually knew that the person they were dealing with was a partner.

If the transaction was entered into with actual or apparent authority on the part of the contracting partner, the firm will be liable. It is likely that there

will be apparent authority on the facts.

explanation.en: The correct answer was C. Although partners are agents of the business and may bind the partnership as individuals, actual and apparent authority need to be considered. Therefore, options A and B are incorrect. Option D is also incorrect – watch out for the exact wording in the question. The third party does not have to show that they actually knew that the person with whom they were dealing was a partner in the firm. They merely need to show that they believed that person to be a partner or had no reason to suspect that they were not. Option E is incorrect as apparent authority is unlikely on the facts.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 2

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 2
stem: A client leaving a partnership has sought advice as to whether she will have any ongoing liability for the partnership’s existing and future debts. The client has already written to the firm’s existing and previous clients informing them of her departure.
ask: Which of the following most accurately describes the position of the client?

options.en: Upon leaving the partnership, the client will automatically cease to be liable for existing and future debts.

The client can avoid liability for existing debts through deeds of release or novation. She can avoid liability for future debts by giving constructive notice

to potential clients and avoiding being held out as a partner.

The client will be liable for existing and future debts unless she enters into deeds of release or novation with the continuing partners and willing

creditors.

Provided that the client gives constructive notice to potential clients and does everything possible to avoid being held out as a partner, she will have no

liability for existing and future debts.
Upon leaving the partnership, the client will automatically cease to be liable for future debts.

explanation.en: The correct answer was B. The client will need to take action to avoid liability for existing and future debts, so options A and E are incorrect. In respect of future debts, the client has already given actual notice to existing and former clients, so needs to give constructive notice and avoid being held out as a partner. As for existing debts, she will need deeds of release or novation. Note that an indemnity will not stop her being liable to the creditors but will entitle the outgoing partner to be indemnified by the continuing partners. Watch out for the fundamental distinction between existing and future debts. Options C and D are incorrect, as they do not make this distinction.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 2

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 3
stem: Two new clients wish to set up a private company limited by shares.
ask: Which of the following best describes the information required in order to complete form IN01?

options.en:
Full details of the shareholders, directors and company secretary (if any), the registered office, the name of the company, how many shares the

company will have, their type and nominal value, and instructions on the articles.

Full details of the shareholders, directors and company secretary (if any), the registered office, the name of the company, its trading name, how many

shares the company will have, their type and nominal value and instructions on the articles.

Full details of the shareholders, directors and company secretary (if any), the registered office, the name of the company, how many shares the

company will have, their type and nominal value, instructions on the articles and details of any service contracts to be issued to the directors.

Full details of the shareholders, directors and company secretary (if any), the registered office, the name of the company, how many shares the

company will have, their type and nominal value, instructions on the articles and confirmation of registration with HMRC.

Full details of the shareholders, directors and company secretary (if any), the registered office, the name of the company, how many shares the

company will have, their type and nominal value, instructions on the articles, confirmation of the auditor and instructions on whether to adopt a company seal.

explanation.en: The correct answer was A. The trading name (option B), directors’ service contracts (option C), registration with HMRC (option D) and whether to have a company seal (option E) can all be decided after incorporation. Depending on the size and value of the company, an auditor may not be required (option E) and their appointment may be decided after incorporation.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 3

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 3
stem: A client was a sole trader who recently incorporated their hairdressing business into a private limited company. They are the sole director and joint and equal shareholder with their spouse. Prior to receiving the certificate of incorporation, the client entered into a contract with a shampoo supplier. The contract was signed by the sole trader on behalf of the company.
ask: With whom, if anyone, does the benefit of the contract reside?

options.en: The company.
The shareholders.
The sole trader.
The sole trader and the company jointly.
The contract is void.

explanation.en: The correct answer was C. The company is not able to enter into contracts until the certificate of incorporation has been issued. Until then, the company can have no liability, so options A and D are incorrect. If made after incorporation, the company would have the benefit of the contract as a separate legal person. The shareholders’ liability would be limited thereafter, but they can have no liability until the company is incorporated, so option B is incorrect. The contract is not void as the sole trader will still be liable by virtue of privity of contract, so option E is incorrect.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 3

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 3
stem: A private limited company was incorporated with unamended model articles of association but has since adopted amended articles.
ask: What must be filed with Companies House following the adoption of the amended articles of association?

options.en: The board minutes relating to the change and the shareholders’ resolution sanctioning the adoption.
The shareholders’ resolution to adopt the amended articles of association only.
The amended articles of association only.
The shareholders’ resolution to adopt the amended articles of association and the amended articles of association.
The board resolution relating to the change and the new articles of association.

explanation.en: The correct answer was D. It is the shareholders who need to pass a special resolution (SR) in general meeting (GM) in order to approve the amendment. Although the directors will usually pass a board resolution (BR) to call the GM, the amendment of the articles is not their decision to make. The company is under a duty to keep minutes of both meetings, but these do not need to be filed at Companies House, so option A is incorrect. BRs and most ordinary resolutions do not need to be filed, but SRs do, so option E is incorrect. Both the SR and the amended articles need to be filed, so options B and C are incorrect.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 3

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 3
stem: A company wishes to call a general meeting to amend the articles of association. There are seven shareholders, all with ordinary voting shares. The client has 52,000 shares, a man has 20,000 shares and a woman has 20,000 shares. The remaining four shareholders have 2,000 shares each.
ask: Which of the following best describes who would be required to agree to hold the meeting on short notice?

options.en: The client, the man and the woman.
Any four – a simple majority in number is required.
The client, the man, the woman and any other shareholder.
The client, as majority shareholder.
The client, the man, the woman and any other two shareholders.

explanation.en: The correct answer was C. In order to satisfy the conditions, there has to be a majority in number of shareholders, who together hold at least 90% of the company’s voting shares. Both pre-conditions have to be satisfied. Option A is incorrect as it does not satisfy the ‘majority in number’ point. Option B is incorrect as it may not satisfy the shareholding threshold. Option D is incorrect as it satisfies neither. Option E exceeds the minimum requirements but could also authorise the decision.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 3

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 3
stem: A client private limited company with unamended model articles of association has six directors and needs to approve the purchase of property worth £3,000 that is jointly owned by two of the directors (the ‘selling directors’). Two directors do not support the transaction, but the remaining four (including the two selling directors and one of the other directors, who is also the chairperson) wish to vote in favour of it.
ask: Which of the following best describes the situation should all directors attend and vote at the board meeting?

options.en: The four directors in favour will be able to pass a board resolution (BR) as they represent the majority.

The four directors in favour will be able to pass a BR as they represent the majority. However, the two selling directors will need to declare their

personal interests in the transaction.

The four directors in favour will be unable to pass the BR. The two selling directors will need to declare their personal interests in the transaction and

will be unable to vote and count towards the quorum.

The four directors in favour will be able to pass the BR. The two selling directors will need to declare their personal interests in the transaction and will

be unable to vote and count towards the quorum. In the event of deadlock (which is anticipated on the facts), the chairperson will be able to exercise her casting vote.
The decision must be authorised by an ordinary resolution of the shareholders.

explanation.en: The correct answer was D. The two selling directors will need to declare their personal interests in the transaction and will be unable to vote and count towards the quorum when the decision is made, so options A, B and C are incorrect. That leaves four directors who are eligible to vote, two in favour and two against. The chairperson will have a casting vote to break the deadlock. An ordinary resolution will not be required as the transaction falls within the directors’ general management powers and is not a substantial property transaction (see Chapter 4). Therefore, option E is incorrect.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 3

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 4
stem: A private limited company with unamended model articles of association wishes to sell some of its land to the father of one of the directors. All of the directors are shareholders. The property has been independently valued at £70,000 and the net asset value of the company is £600,000.
ask: Does the proposed sale of land require shareholder approval?

options.en: No, because the property has been independently valued.
Yes, because the transaction is more than 10% of the company’s net asset value.
Yes, because the company’s directors are also shareholders.
No, because the transaction falls within the directors’ general management powers.
No, because the transaction does not exceed £100,000.

explanation.en: The correct answer was B. The independent valuation is not a factor in determining whether shareholder approval is required (option A), neither is the fact that all shareholders are directors (option C) (although an SPT must be between the company and a director/someone connected with a director). The transaction would fall within general management powers (option D) if it were not an SPT as defined. Option E is incorrect as if the value of the transaction is more than £5,000, but up to and including £100,000, it may still be an SPT if it is more than 10% of the company’s net asset value.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 4

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 4
stem: A private limited company with unamended model articles of association and a net asset value of £85,000 wishes to enter into some property transactions. The finance director has agreed to buy a van from the company, for the sum of £3,000. The brother of the marketing director has agreed to sell an investment property to the company for the sum of £150,000. Finally, the company has agreed to purchase freehold premises for £90,000 from another company in which the sales director has a 15% shareholding and his wife has a 10% shareholding.
ask: Which of the following best describes the required resolutions to authorise these transactions?

options.en: A board resolution for the van and ordinary resolutions for the investment property and freehold premises.
Ordinary resolutions for the van, investment property and freehold premises.
Board resolutions for the van and investment property and an ordinary resolution for the freehold premises.
Board resolutions for the van, investment property and freehold premises.
A board resolution for the van and freehold premises and an ordinary resolution for the investment property.

explanation.en: The correct answer was C. A board resolution is required for the van as the value is £5,000 or less, even though the transaction involves a director. Therefore, option B is incorrect on this point. An ordinary resolution is required for the freehold premises as the director is connected with the selling company (he and his wife, a connected person, own at least 20% of the shares) and the value exceeds 10% of the purchasing company’s net asset value. Options D and E are wrong here. A board resolution is required for the investment property as, despite the value, siblings are not connected persons in the context of SPTs. Therefore, options A, B and E are incorrect in this respect.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 4

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 4
stem: A private limited company with unamended model articles of association wishes to grant a two-year guaranteed fixed-term service contract to an existing director.
ask: Which of the following best describes the required formalities?

options.en:
A board resolution will be required. The director will need to declare his interest in the proposed transaction, will be unable to vote, and will not count

towards the quorum when the decision is made.

An ordinary resolution will be required. In the board meeting that follows, the director will need to declare his interest in the proposed transaction, will

be unable to vote and will not count towards the quorum when the decision is made.

An ordinary resolution will be required. In the board meeting that follows, the director will not need to declare his interest in the proposed transaction

but will be unable to vote and will not count towards the quorum when the decision is made.

An ordinary resolution will be required. In the board meeting that follows, the director will not need to declare his interest in the proposed transaction,

will be able to vote and will count towards the quorum when the decision is made.

A board resolution will be required. The director will not need to declare his interest in the proposed transaction but will be unable to vote, and will not

count towards the quorum when the decision is made.

explanation.en: The correct answer was E. An ordinary resolution will not be required as the service contract is not for a guaranteed term of more than two years. Therefore, options B, C and D are incorrect on this point. The director will not be required to declare his interest as there is an exception to the general rule that applies, where a director’s service contract is being considered (s 177(6)(c) CA), therefore options A and B are incorrect here. The director will not be able to vote and count towards the quorum of the board meeting, so option D is also incorrect here.

stem: A director of a private company, limited by shares, has taken, for their own personal benefit, a contract that was initially being negotiated by the company. The same director has also been awarded an excessive pay rise and the company has persistently failed to pay dividends when profits are available. The client, who has a 25% shareholding in the company, wishes to take action.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en:
The director has potentially breached the duty to avoid conflicts of interest. The directors may authorise a breach of this duty by board resolution, but

the interested director’s vote will not count. The client could remove the director from office.

The director has potentially breached the duty to avoid conflicts of interest. The directors may authorise a breach of this duty by board resolution, but

the interested director’s vote will not count. The client may take derivative action or seek relief for unfairly prejudicial conduct.

The director has potentially breached the duty to declare an interest in a transaction. The client may take derivative action or seek relief for unfairly

prejudicial conduct.

The director has potentially breached the duty to avoid conflicts of interest. The directors may authorise a breach of this duty by board resolution, but

the interested director’s vote will not count. The client may take derivative action or seek to remove the director from office.

The director has potentially breached the duty to avoid conflicts of interest. The directors may authorise a breach of this duty by board resolution, but

the interested director’s vote will not count. The client may seek relief for unfairly prejudicial conduct or seek to remove the director from office.

explanation.en: The correct answer was B. The client could not remove the director from office based on their voting power alone, as they are a minority shareholder. Therefore, options A, D and E are incorrect in this respect. On the facts, there has been no breach of the duty to declare an interest in a proposed transaction, so option C is incorrect. Option D also fails to mention the possibility of a petition for unfairly prejudicial conduct, option E does not mention a derivative action, and option A does not mention either of them. Both are relevant on the facts.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 4

stem: A director of a private company limited by shares negotiated a contract that caused the company a significant loss. Since then, the director has cut outgoings, personally authorised all expenses to make sure they are strictly necessary and made some redundancies. The director checks the accounts on a daily basis, but despite the director’s best efforts, the company loses a lucrative contract and becomes insolvent.
ask: Which of the following best sets out the position of the director?

options.en: The director may be liable for wrongful trading but is likely to have a defence on the facts.
The director may be liable for wrongful trading and fraudulent trading.
The director may be liable for wrongful trading.
The director may be liable for fraudulent trading.
The director may be liable for misfeasance.

explanation.en: The correct answer was A. Although there is the potential for wrongful trading here, the director is likely to have a defence, as they could argue that they took every step to minimise potential loss to creditors as ought to have been taken. Therefore, options B and C are incorrect here. The director is unlikely to have had an intention to defraud here, so fraudulent trading is unlikely (as suggested in options B and D). Misfeasance is also unlikely here as there is no clear breach of directors’ duties, so option E is incorrect.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 4

stem: Five years ago, a company created a floating charge over its entire undertaking in favour of a bank. Three years later, the company completed a debenture in favour of a lender, which created a floating charge over all of its assets. The lender was aware of the prior charge, but it was not registered at Companies House. Both charges were duly executed by the parties and the lender’s charge was registered at Companies House. The company is now in insolvent liquidation.
ask: Which of the following best describes the position?

options.en: The lender’s charge takes priority as the bank’s charge is void against the liquidator and the lender.
The lender’s charge takes priority as the bank’s charge is void against the liquidator.
The bank’s charge takes priority, because the lender had actual notice of the prior charge.
The bank’s charge takes priority, because the date of creation determines the order of priority.
The bank’s charge takes priority, because the date of creation determines the order of priority and registration is voluntary.

explanation.topic: Financing a business, financial records and accounting requirements
explanation.en: The correct answer was A. The lender’s charge takes priority as the bank’s charge is void against the liquidator and the lender, due to non- registration. Option B is wrong as the charge is void against both the liquidator and the lender. Notice is not a factor in the priority between floating charges, so option C is wrong. Although the date of creation determines the order of priority, this is subject to registration, and although registration is voluntary, non-registration still has serious consequences. Therefore, options D and E are incorrect.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 5

stem: A company has a fixed charge over its freehold premises and a floating charge over its stock. Both charges were duly executed and registered and the fixed charge was granted first. The company is not in breach of either charge and is solvent.
ask: Which of the following best describes the position as to dealing with the assets?

options.en: The company may sell the freehold premises and stock without recourse to the lender(s).
The company may sell the freehold premises but will need the bank’s consent. It may sell the stock when the floating charge has crystallised.
The company may sell the freehold premises but will need the bank’s consent. It may sell the stock without recourse to the bank.

The company may sell the freehold premises but the bank will need to be added as a party to the sale. It may sell the stock when the floating charge

has crystallised.

The company may sell the freehold premises but will need the bank’s consent. It may sell the stock without recourse to the bank unless and until

crystallisation occurs.

explanation.topic: Financing a business, financial records and accounting requirements
explanation.en: The correct answer was E. This is because the lender’s consent will be required for the sale of the premises, but the bank will not need to be added as a party to the sale as it does not have legal title to the property. Therefore, options A and D are wrong. It will be able to deal with the stock, freely, until crystallisation. Therefore options A, B, C and D are incorrect in this respect.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 5

stem: A private limited company, formed in December 2010, with model articles of association and 100,000 ordinary shares, wishes to issue 50,000 new ordinary shares for cash. All of the shareholders are directors. Since incorporation, there have been no resolutions authorising the issue of shares.
ask: Which of the following best describes the position?

options.en: The board can issue the shares without recourse to the members.
The members can issue the shares without reference to the board.

An ordinary resolution will be required to authorise the issue of shares and a special resolution will be required to disapply the statutory pre-emption

rights.

An ordinary resolution will not be required to authorise the issue of shares, but a special resolution will be required to disapply the statutory pre-

emption rights.

An ordinary resolution will not be required to authorise the issue of shares and a special resolution will not be required to disapply the statutory pre-

emption rights.

explanation.topic: Financing a business, financial records and accounting requirements
explanation.en: The correct answer was D. This is because an ordinary resolution will not be required to authorise the issue as the company has only one class of shares. However, a special resolution will be required to disapply the statutory pre-emption rights as shares are being issued for cash. Therefore options A, C and E are incorrect. Option B is also incorrect as it is the directors who issue shares.
