stem: A private limited company with unamended model articles of association wishes to authorise the purchase of some of its own shares for the sum of £50,000. Distributable profits are £200,000 and net assets are £1m.
ask: Which of the following best describes the position?

options.en: A special resolution will be required to authorise the purchase out of capital.

The company may choose to purchase the shares out of profits, by way of ordinary resolution, or to purchase them out of capital, for which a special

resolution will be required.
The company may only purchase the shares out of profits and an ordinary resolution will be required.
The company may only purchase the shares out of profits and a special resolution will be required.
An ordinary resolution will be required to authorise the purchase out of profits.

explanation.topic: Financing a business, financial records and accounting requirements
explanation.en:
The correct answer was C. This is because the company may not purchase shares out of capital, as profits are available, so option A is incorrect. An ordinary resolution will be required. The company does not have a choice in these circumstances, so option B is incorrect. Option E is technically correct, but the additional detail in option C makes the position clearer and thus option C is the better answer. Option D is incorrect as it says that a

special resolution is required. For a purchase out of capital, an ordinary resolution is required to approve the contract, in addition to the special resolution to use capital.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 5

stem: A business has fixed assets of £200,000, current assets of £40,000, current liabilities of £20,000 and long-term liabilities of £100,000.
ask: Which of the following best describes the position?

options.en: Net assets are £20,000 and net current assets are £120,000.
Net assets are £120,000 and net current assets are £20,000.
Net assets are £100,000 and net current assets are £20,000.
Net assets are £20,000 and net current assets are £100,000.
Net assets are £300,000 and net current assets are £60,000.

explanation.topic: Financing a business, financial records and accounting requirements
explanation.en: The correct answer was B. This is because current assets less current liabilities = net current assets. Total assets less total liabilities = net assets. Option A is incorrect as the figures are the wrong way around. Option C is incorrect as it deducted long-term liabilities from fixed assets. Option D used the same incorrect figures for net current assets and net assets. Option E is incorrect as it added together the incorrect figures.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 5

stem: A bankruptcy order is made against a client, who is a sole trader. They have no secured debt, but owe money to an employee, trade supplier, HMRC and their civil partner.
ask: Which of the following are potentially preferential creditors?

options.en: The employee only.
The employee, trade supplier and civil partner.
The employee, HMRC and trade supplier.
The employee and HMRC.
HMRC and the trade supplier.

explanation.en: The correct answer was D. The employee is primary preferential creditor and HMRC is secondary preferential creditor. The trade supplier will be an ordinary creditor and the civil partner will be a postponed creditor (so options B, C and E are incorrect). Option A also omits HMRC and option E omits the employee.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 6

stem: A bankruptcy order is made against a man this month, following presentation of a bankruptcy petition in the previous month.
ask: Which of the following most accurately describes a potential preference(s)?

options.en: A gift of £10,000, made to the man’s friend, 12 months ago.
Repayment of a loan of £5,000 to the man’s sister, 18 months ago.
The sale of a property, for £120,000 less than its then market value, to the man’s son, four years ago.
Full repayment of his credit card balance, one year ago.
Repayment of a loan of £5,000 to the man’s sister, 18 months ago and full repayment of his credit card balance, one year ago.

explanation.en: The correct answer was B. The man’s sister is his associate. Provided that he was insolvent at the time or because of the transaction and had a desire to prefer, it will be voidable. Desire to prefer will be presumed in the circumstances. Options A and C are potential undervalues. Although a potential preference, option D is out of time as it is to an unconnected person (also making option E incorrect).
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 6

stem: A company’s assets exceed its liabilities, and it is generally able to pay its debts as they fall due. However, a statutory demand for an unsecured debt of £6,000 was served four weeks ago by a creditor and has not been complied with. The company has also not made an application to set it aside.
ask: Which of the following best describes the position?

options.en: The creditor may petition for the winding-up of the company.
The company is able to pay its debts under insolvency legislation.
The company is unable to pay its debts under insolvency legislation and the creditor may petition for the winding-up of the company.
The company is unable to pay its debts under insolvency legislation, so the company will be wound up.
The company is able to pay its debts under insolvency legislation as assets exceed liabilities and technically it can pay its debts as they fall due.

explanation.en: The correct answer was C. Option A is partially correct, but omitted reference to insolvency legislation. Options B and E are incorrect as even though the company appears solvent, non-compliance with the statutory demand deems the company unable to pay its debts. Option D is incorrect as it omits the need for a winding-up petition.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 6

Of the liabilities, £50,000 is owed to preferential creditors and there are no floating charge holders. The client is owed £50,000 as an unsecured creditor.
ask: Which of the following best sets out what the client will receive?

options.en: £0.50 for every £1.

explanation.en: The correct answer was E. Preferential creditors are paid first, which reduces assets and liabilities by £50,000. 150,000/350,000 = 0.42857143 x £50,000 = £21,428.57. Options A and C are incorrect as they do not take into account the preferential creditors. Options B and D are incorrect as they reduced only the liabilities and assets figures respectively by £50,000.

stem: A bankruptcy order is made against a client, who is the joint owner of the matrimonial home.
ask: Which of the following best describes the position?

options.en: All of the client’s property will vest in the trustee in bankruptcy. A court order will be required to sell the home.

All of the client’s property will vest in the trustee in bankruptcy except for tools of the trade and most items essential for day-to-day living. A court

order will not be required to sell the home.

All of the client’s property will vest in the trustee in bankruptcy except for tools of the trade, their interest in the home, and most items essential for

day-to-day living. A court order will be required to sell the home.

All of the client’s property will vest in the trustee in bankruptcy except for tools of the trade, their interest in the home, and most items essential for

day-to-day living. A court order will not be required to sell the home.

All of the client’s property will vest in the trustee in bankruptcy except for tools of the trade and most items essential for day-to-day living. A court

order will be required to sell the home.

explanation.en: The correct answer was E. Option A is incorrect as it did not exclude tools of the trade and day-to-day items. Options B and D are incorrect as a court order will be required. Options C and D are also incorrect as they suggest that the bankrupt’s share of the home will not pass to the trustee in bankruptcy.

stem: In an accounting period, a company buys stock totalling £750,000, which it sells for £2m. It pays wages of £100,000 and other bills of £80,000 and buys new freehold premises and cars for £200,000 and £50,000 respectively.
ask: Ignoring any capital allowances, what are the company’s trading profits?

explanation.en: The correct answer was B. The cars and freehold premises are not deductible expenses as they are of a capital nature, rather than an income nature. Option A is incorrect as it deducted all figures from the sales. Option C is incorrect as it did not deduct any expenses other than the purchases. Option D is incorrect as it deducted everything except the premises (incorrectly deducting the cars as an expense) and option E is incorrect as it deducted everything except the cars (incorrectly deducting the premises as an expense).

stem: A sole trader buys new plant and machinery costing £2m and has an existing pool of plant and machinery with a written down value of £1m in the previous financial year.
ask: Which of the following best describes the capital allowances the sole trader will be able to claim?

options.en: The sole trader will be able to claim 14% of the cost of the new plant and machinery and 14% of the written down value of the existing pool.
The sole trader will be able to claim the cost of the new plant and machinery and 14% of the written down value of the existing pool.
The sole trader will be able to claim the cost of the new plant and machinery up to £1m and 14% of the written down value of the existing pool.

The sole trader will be able to claim the cost of the new plant and machinery up to £1m, 40% relief on the balance of £1m, and 14% of the written down

value of the existing pool.
The sole trader will be able to claim the cost of the new plant and machinery up to £1m and 40% relief on the balance of £1m.

explanation.en: The correct answer was D. Option B is incorrect due to the cap of £1m on the annual investment allowance and the limit on the first year allowance. Option E is incorrect as it fails to take into account the writing down allowance on the existing plant and machinery. Option C is incorrect as it fails to take into account the first year allowance on the remaining cost of the new plant and machinery. Option A is incorrect as it fails to take into account the annual investment allowance and first year allowance.

stem: A sole trader makes a trading loss in the first year of trade, a profit in their second year of trade and a loss in their final year of trade. Prior to setting up the business, they had salary income for several years and they continue to receive a salary of £10,000 per annum for consultancy work.
ask: Which of the following best describes the reliefs that may be available for the trading losses?

options.en: Start-up loss relief, carry-across relief, carry-back relief and carry-forward relief.
Start-up loss relief and terminal loss relief.
Start-up loss relief, terminal loss relief and carry-forward relief on incorporation.
Carry-across relief, carry-back relief and carry-forward relief.
Start-up loss relief, carry-across relief, carry-back relief, carry-forward relief and terminal loss relief.

explanation.en: The correct answer was E. All of the other options omit at least one of these reliefs. Option C is also incorrect as carry-forward relief on incorporation is irrelevant to the facts.

stem: A client sets up business as a private medical doctor and works exclusively in providing medical diagnosis and treatment. In their first year of business, the client made trading profits of £100,000.
ask: Which of the following best describes the client’s VAT position in their second year of business?

options.en: The client must register for VAT as their taxable profits in the previous year exceeded £90,000.
The client does not need to register for VAT as they make only exempt supplies. The client will be unable to recover any input tax paid.
The client does not need to register for VAT as they make only zero-rated supplies.
The client does not need to register for VAT as they make only exempt supplies. The client will be able to recover any input tax paid.
The client must register for VAT as their taxable profits in the previous year exceeded £90,000. The client will be able to recover any input tax paid.

explanation.en: The correct answer was B. The client does not need to register as they make only exempt supplies, so options A and E are incorrect. They do not make zero-rated supplies, so option C is incorrect. Businesses that make only zero-rated supplies may apply for registration for VAT and may recover input tax paid. The client will be unable to recover any input tax paid, so options D and E are also incorrect on this point.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 7

stem: A client, who is a taxable person and registered for VAT, buys raw materials for £100 plus VAT and sells the finished products for £300 plus VAT.
ask: Assuming VAT is chargeable at the standard rate, which of the following best describes the client’s VAT liability?

explanation.en: The correct answer was A. Input tax at 20% of £100 (£20) may be deducted from output tax of 20% of £300 (£60). Option B is incorrect as it did not deduct the input tax and option C is incorrect as it added the input tax to the output tax. Options D and E are incorrect as they applied the rates of 17.5% and 12.5% respectively.

stem: A client has a taxable salary of £41,000 and receives a gross dividend of £5,000 on shares that they own in a limited company. They have no other income.
ask: How much income tax, if any, should the client pay on the dividend?

options.en: The client will have to pay tax at the additional rate on the proportion of the dividend that exceeds their dividend allowance.
The client will have to pay tax at the ordinary rate as the dividend does not exceed the basic rate threshold.

The client will have to pay tax at the ordinary rate as the dividend does not exceed the basic rate threshold. However, the first £500 will be taxed at

0%.
The client will have to pay tax at the ordinary rate on the entire dividend because it exceeds their dividend allowance.
The client will have to pay tax at the upper rate on £4,500 of the dividend. The first £500 will be taxed at 0%.

explanation.en: The correct answer was E. This is because their taxable salary already exceeds the basic rate band. The client is into the upper rate for the dividend (not the additional rate as suggested in option A, or the ordinary rate as suggested in options B, C and D). Option B is also incorrect, because it does not mention the dividend allowance and option D does not explain it correctly.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 8

stem: A client has a total salary of £65,000 and pays interest of £100 on a loan to buy a share in a partnership. The client receives a gross dividend of £3,000 and gross interest of £1,000 on their savings. The personal allowance is £12,570 and the higher rate threshold for taxable income is £37,700.
ask: Which of the following best describes the client’s liability for income tax?

options.en:
The client is a higher rate taxpayer (HRT) and their basic rate band has been fully used up by their taxable salary. They will pay tax on the interest

received and dividend at the higher/upper rates.

The client is an HRT with taxable income of £56,330 and their basic rate band has been fully used up by their taxable salary. They will pay tax on the

interest received and dividend at the higher/upper rates, but the first £500 of the interest will be taxed at 0% and the first £500 of the dividend will be taxed at 0%.

The client is an HRT with taxable income of £56,330 and their basic rate band has been fully used up by their taxable salary. They will pay tax on the

dividend at the higher/upper rates, but the interest received will be taxed at 0% as it falls within the personal savings allowance and the first £500 of the dividend will be taxed at 0%.

The client is an HRT with taxable income of £56,430 and their basic rate band has been fully used up by their taxable salary. They will pay tax on the

interest and dividend at the higher/upper rates, but the first £500 of the interest will be taxed at 0% and the first £500 of the dividend will be taxed at 0%.

The client will not be liable to tax on the interest as it does not exceed £5,000. They will pay tax at a rate of 10.75% on £1,000 of the dividend as it

does not exceed £37,700, but the first £500 of the dividend will be taxed at 0%.

explanation.en: The correct answer was B. The taxable income figure in option D is incorrect, as it does not take into account the allowable relief. As a higher rate taxpayer, the dividend allowance (DA) will be £500 and the personal savings allowance (PSA) will be £500, not £1,000, as suggested in option C. Option A is incorrect as it ignores the PSA and DA. Option E is incorrect, as it does not take into account the progressive nature of income tax.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 8

sourceTitle: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 8
stem: A client has taxable non-savings/non-dividend income of £35,000 and receives gross interest of £6,000 on their savings. They have no other income.
ask: What rate(s) of tax will they be required to pay on the interest?

explanation.en: The correct answer was C. Taxable non-savings/non-dividend income (NSNDI) means that the personal allowance and any allowable reliefs have already been deducted. Taxable NSNDI of £35,000 and taxable savings income of £6,000 means that the client is a higher rate taxpayer, so they will be entitled to a personal savings allowance of £500, taxable at 0% (not £1,000 as suggested in option D). They will be taxed on the balance of £2,200 at 20% and the balance of £3,300 at 40%. All of the other options state the incorrect rate(s) and/or ignore the crossover between rates.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 8

stem: A client has taxable non-savings/non-dividend income of £38,000 and no savings income. They receive a gross dividend of £2,000.
ask: How much tax will they be required to pay on the dividend?

explanation.en: The correct answer was A. Taxable non-savings/non-dividend income (NSNDI) means that the personal allowance and any allowable reliefs have already been deducted. Taxable NSNDI of £38,000 and taxable dividend income of £2,000 means that the client is a higher rate taxpayer, so they will be entitled to a dividend allowance of £500, taxable at 0%. They will be taxed on the balance of £1,500 at 35.75%. Option B is incorrect as it suggests the dividend allowance is £1,000. Option C is incorrect as it calculates the tax at 10.75%. Options D and E are incorrect as they both ignore the dividend allowance and charge the whole amount to tax at 10.75% and 35.75% respectively.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 8

stem: A client is concerned about potential liability under the general anti-abuse rule (GAAR) and penalties for late payment of income tax.
ask: Which of the following best describes the position?

options.en:
Under the GAAR procedure, a taxpayer will be notified if an abusive tax avoidance arrangement (ATAA) is uncovered and a fine may be payable.

Penalties for late payment include interest and fixed penalties.

Under the GAAR procedure, a taxpayer will be notified if an ATAA is uncovered and a request for tax adjustments will be made. Penalties for late

payment include interest and fixed penalties.

Under the GAAR procedure, a taxpayer will be notified if an ATAA is uncovered, a fine may be payable and a request for tax adjustments will be made.

Penalties for late payment include interest and fixed penalties.

Under the GAAR, HMRC must notify a taxpayer before imposing a fine. The GAAR advisory panel deals with any representations made by the taxpayer.

Penalties for late payment are limited to payment of interest.

Any breach of GAAR will automatically be referred to a tax tribunal, which will consider any representations made by a taxpayer. Penalties for late

payment include interest and fixed penalties.

explanation.en: The correct answer was B. Fines are not payable under the GAAR (as suggested in options A, C and D), but a request for tax adjustments may be made. Penalties for late payment include interest and fixed penalties, which also makes option D incorrect. Breaches of the GAAR are not automatically referred to a tax tribunal, as suggested in option E.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 8

topicTags: Capital gains tax and inheritance tax
stem: A client, who is a sole trader, purchased their business (which included a freehold commercial property) 10 years ago for £100,000. The client has now retired and has sold the business for £200,000. They have not made any previous capital disposals.
ask: Which of the following will the client be able to deduct from the sale price in order to calculate their basic gain?

options.en:
The purchase price, estate agents’ fees of £3,750 incurred in the sale, £2,500 spent repairing the roof, £3,000 in legal fees on the sale, £2,000 in legal

fees on the purchase and £4,000 in installing a replacement kitchen and windows.
Estate agents’ fees of £3,750 incurred in the sale, £3,000 in legal fees on the sale and £2,000 in legal fees on the purchase.
The purchase price, estate agents’ fees of £3,750 incurred in the sale, £3,000 in legal fees on the sale and £2,000 in legal fees on the purchase.

The purchase price, estate agents’ fees of £3,750 incurred in the sale, £3,000 in legal fees on the sale, £2,000 in legal fees on the purchase and

£4,000 in installing a replacement kitchen and windows.

Estate agents’ fees of £3,750 incurred in the sale, £3,000 in legal fees on the sale, £2,000 in legal fees on the purchase and £4,000 in installing a

replacement kitchen and windows.

explanation.topic: Capital gains tax and inheritance tax
explanation.en: The correct answer was C. This is because the purchase price must be deducted (which is why option B is incorrect and partially why option E is incorrect). The other items listed are allowable expenditure. Options A, D and E are incorrect, as repair/replacement/renewal of existing items does not usually qualify as allowable expenditure.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 9

topicTags: Capital gains tax and inheritance tax
stem: A client is selling their 25% ordinary shareholding in a trading company for £2m. They bought the shares 20 years ago for £500,000 and they carry 25% of the voting rights in the company. You can assume that there is no allowable expenditure. The client was a director of the company, until they retired five years ago. The client is a higher rate taxpayer (HRT) and has only made one other capital disposal, three years ago, where they claimed business asset disposal relief (BADR) on a chargeable gain of £200,000.
ask: Which of the following best describes the client’s liability for capital gains tax (CGT)?

options.en: The client will be entitled to the full annual exemption (AE) and to BADR on the chargeable gain. CGT will be charged at 24%, as the client is an HRT.

The client will be entitled to the full AE and to BADR on the chargeable gain, up to £1m. CGT will be charged at 24% on the balance, as the client is an

HRT.

The client will be entitled to the full AE and to BADR on the chargeable gain up to £800,000. CGT will be charged at 24% on the balance, as the client

is an HRT.
The client will be entitled to the full AE and to BADR on the chargeable gain. CGT will be payable at a rate of 18%.
The client will be entitled to the full AE, but not to BADR. CGT will be payable at a rate of 24% as the client is an HRT.

explanation.topic: Capital gains tax and inheritance tax
explanation.en: The correct answer was E. The AE applies as the client has not made any previous capital disposals in the current tax year. However, BADR does not apply (as assumed in options A–D) as they fail to satisfy the condition of being an employee or officer of the company for the last two years. Options A, B and D are also incorrect, as if BADR had been available, they would have been taxed at a flat rate of 18% for the first £800,000 (bearing in mind the lifetime limit of £1m) and 24% on the balance. Option C would have been correct if all conditions for BADR had been satisfied.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 9

topicTags: Capital gains tax and inheritance tax
stem: A trading partnership has three partners (a man, a woman and a client) who have been in partnership for five years. They share income profits equally and capital profits in accordance with their capital contributions, which are as follows: Man: 50% Woman: 30% Client: 20% Four years ago, the firm purchased office premises for £100,000, and they have just been sold for £200,000. None of the partners have made any previous capital disposals and they are all higher rate taxpayers.
ask: Which of the following best describes the partners’ liability to capital gains tax (CGT) on the sale?

options.en:
Each partner will pay CGT on the percentage of the basic gain that corresponds with the proportion in which they share capital profits. They will be

entitled to deduct any allowable expenditure and the annual exemption first and it is likely they will qualify for BADR, paying tax at 18%.

Each partner will pay CGT on the percentage of the basic gain that corresponds with the proportion in which they share capital profits. They will be

entitled to deduct the annual exemption first, but it is unlikely that they will qualify for BADR.

Each partner will be liable to pay CGT on one-third of the basic gain. They will be entitled to deduct any allowable expenditure and the annual

exemption first and it is likely they will qualify for BADR, paying tax at 18%.

Each partner will be liable to pay CGT on one-third of the basic gain. They will be entitled to deduct any allowable expenditure and the annual

exemption first, but it is unlikely they will qualify for BADR, so they will pay tax at 24%.

Each partner will pay CGT on the percentage of the basic gain that corresponds with the proportion in which they share in capital profits. They will be

entitled to deduct any allowable expenditure and the annual exemption first and it is likely they will qualify for BADR, paying tax at 24%, as higher rate taxpayers.

explanation.topic: Capital gains tax and inheritance tax
explanation.en: The correct answer was A. The express agreement sets the share of capital profits, which displaces the presumption of equal shares. Therefore, options C and D are incorrect. The allowable expenditure and annual exemption can be deducted. Option B is incorrect as it fails to mention the allowable expenditure and suggests BADR will not apply (as does option D). BADR applies as they have owned the business for at least two years and it gives a flat rate of 18% (not 24%, as suggested in option E). They are clearly within their lifetime limit, having not made any previous capital disposals.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 9

stem: A client sold their holiday home in England two weeks ago. The client is a higher rate taxpayer and the property has never been let commercially. The property was bought for £400,000 five years ago and is now being sold for £700,000. Legal fees of £1,500 were paid on the acquisition, and solicitors’ and estate agents’ fees together totalling £3,500 have been incurred on the sale. Three years ago, the client built a substantial extension costing £100,000. The current annual exemption is £3,000 and the client has made no previous capital disposals.
ask: Which of the following best identifies the client’s capital gains tax liability?

explanation.topic: Capital gains tax and inheritance tax
explanation.en: The correct answer was E. £700,000 – £400,000 – £1,500 – £3,500 – £100,000 – £3,000 = £192,000 chargeable gain. This is taxed at 24% as the client is a higher rate taxpayer. Option A is incorrect, as the cost of the extension was not deducted, and tax was charged at 20%. Option B is incorrect as tax was charged at 20%. Option C is incorrect as tax was charged at 10%. Option D is incorrect, as the cost of the extension was not deducted. The transaction does not qualify for business asset disposal relief as it is not business property.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 9

topicTags: Capital gains tax and inheritance tax
stem: A client who was a 50% partner in an accountancy business dies. He purchased his share in the business 10 years ago for £200,000 and it is now worth £350,000. He also owned, for eight years, business premises that were occupied by the business. There is no binding contract for sale of these assets in the partnership agreement.
ask: Which of the following best describes the tax position in respect of the business interest and the premises?

options.en: The personal representatives will pay capital gains tax (CGT) on the market value of the business interest and the chargeable gain on the premises.
The personal representatives will pay CGT on the chargeable gain of the business interest and the premises.

No CGT will be payable, but the personal representatives will acquire the business interest and the premises at their market value as at the date of the

client’s death. Inheritance tax will be payable.

No CGT will be payable, but the personal representatives will acquire the business interest and the premises at their market value as at the date of the

client’s death. It is likely that business property relief (BPR) of 100% will apply to the business interest and BPR of 50% will apply to the premises.

No CGT will be payable, but the personal representatives will acquire the business interest and the premises at their market value as at the date of the

client’s death. It is likely that BPR of 100% will apply to the business interest and the premises.

explanation.topic: Capital gains tax and inheritance tax
explanation.en: The correct answer was D. There is no liability to CGT on death, so options A and B are incorrect. Option C is partially correct, but does not acknowledge BPR. BPR is correctly applied in option D, but incorrectly applied in option E.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 9

stem: A man has a 40% shareholding in a trading company with four shareholders. Two of the other shareholders each own 28% of the shares and the remaining shareholder holds 4%. All shareholders are full-time working directors of the company. In the current financial year, the company makes trading profits and chargeable gains (after indexation) totalling £1.7m. The company pays directors’ fees of £300,000, dividends of £700,000 and debenture interest of £100,000. It also makes a loan of £10,000 to the remaining shareholder.
ask: Which of the following best describes the company’s corporation tax liability and the position with the loan?

options.en:
The directors’ fees, dividends and debenture interest are deductible expenses. A deposit must be paid to HMRC in respect of the loan, as this is a

close company.
The directors’ fees and debenture interest are deductible expenses. A deposit must be paid to HMRC in respect of the loan, as this is a close company.

The directors’ fees, debenture interest and loan are deductible expenses. No deposit must be paid to HMRC in respect of the loan as it falls within one

of the exceptions under the close company rules.

The directors’ fees, dividends, debenture interest and loan are deductible expenses. No deposit must be paid to HMRC in respect of the loan as it falls

within one of the exceptions under the close company rules.

The directors’ fees and debenture interest are deductible expenses. No deposit must be paid to HMRC in respect of the loan as it falls within one of

the exceptions under the close company rules.

explanation.en: The correct answer was E. The dividends (options A and D) and loan (options C and D) are not deductible expenses. No deposit is payable, as although this is a close company, one of the exceptions applies. Therefore, options A and B are incorrect in this respect.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 10

stem: In its first 12-month accounting period of trade, a company makes neither a trading profit nor a trading loss, but did make a chargeable gain (and no overall capital loss) from the sale of a freehold property. In the second 12-month accounting period, a trading loss was made and there was no capital gain or capital loss. In the third (but not final) accounting period, a trading profit was made and there was no capital gain or capital loss.
ask: Which of the following best describes the corporation tax relief(s) that may be available to the company?

options.en: Carry-across, carry-back and carry-forward.
Carry-across and carry-forward.
Carry-back and carry-forward.
Carry-back, carry-forward and terminal carry-back.
Carry-forward and terminal carry-back.

explanation.en: The correct answer was C. Carry-across does not apply (as suggested in options A and B) as the company made no other profits in the loss-making year. Terminal carry-back does not apply (as suggested in options D and E) as the company has not ceased to trade.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 10

stem: A company makes income profits of £800,000 and a chargeable gain (after indexation) of £900,000 in the same tax year. The directors are considering whether to pay dividends of £500,000 or directors’ fees of £500,000.
ask: Which of the following best describes the tax position?

options.en: The company will pay income tax on the income profits and capital gains tax on the chargeable gain.
The company will pay corporation tax on the income profits and chargeable gain. The dividends and directors’ fees are deductible expenses.

The company will pay income tax on the income profits and capital gains tax on the chargeable gain. The dividends and directors’ fees are deductible

expenses.
The company will pay corporation tax on the income profits and chargeable gain. The directors’ fees are deductible expenses.

The shareholders and directors will pay income tax on their dividends and directors’ fees respectively, and the company will pay corporation tax on the

income profits.

explanation.en: The correct answer was D. Companies do not pay income tax or capital gains tax (as suggested in options A and C). Dividends are not deductible expenses for corporation tax purposes, so options B and C are incorrect. Although income tax is payable by individuals on dividends and directors’ fees, corporation tax is payable on both a company’s income profits and chargeable gains, so option E is incorrect.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 10

stem: A company makes income profits of £600,000 and a chargeable gain (after indexation) of £1m in the same tax year. The company pays directors’ fees of £400,000 and pays debenture interest of £50,000.
ask: Which of the following accurately states the company’s corporation tax liability?

explanation.en: The correct answer was A (£600,000 + £1,000,000 – £400,000 – £50,000 x 25%). Option B is incorrect as it does not deduct the directors’ fees and debenture interest. Option C is incorrect as it does not deduct the debenture interest. Option D is incorrect as it does not deduct the directors’ fees. Option E is incorrect because it applies corporation tax at 19%.

stem: In its third 12-month accounting period of trade, a company makes a trading profit from manufacturing, but a trading loss from its property portfolio (which made a profit in the second accounting period). It made no chargeable gain or loss in the same periods. In the fourth and final 12- month accounting period, trading profits were made for both parts of the business and there were no capital gains or capital losses.
ask: Which of the following best describes the potential corporation tax relief(s) that may be available to the company?

options.en: Carry-across, terminal carry-back and carry-forward.
Carry-forward and terminal carry-back.
Carry-across and carry-forward.
Carry-back, carry-forward and terminal carry-back.
Carry-across, carry-back and carry-forward.

explanation.en: The correct answer was E. On the facts, all three reliefs may be an option and all other options omit one or more of them. Carry-across could be used for the trading loss in the third year, even though it relates to a different part of the business. Carry-back could be used against the trading profit in year two. Carry-forward could be used against the trading profit in year four. Terminal carry-back relief could not be used (as suggested in options A, B and D) as although the company is ceasing to trade, it did not make a loss in the final 12 months of trade.
explanation.source: Revise SQE 2027 · Business Law and Practice · Chapter 10
